lists.title: Tagalog A1 Grammar Path
lists.description: First Tagalog: the ang/ng/sa marker system, actor-focus verbs with -um-, the na linker, the mga plural marker, may/wala existence and possession, and hindi negation.

lists.title: Tagalog A2 Grammar Path
lists.description: The focus system opens up: mag- beside -um-, the three aspects, object focus with -in and locative focus with -an, the ang/ng/sa pronoun sets, si and sina for names, questions with ba, and ma- adjectives with their linker.

lists.title: Tagalog B1 Grammar Path
lists.description: i- focus for things given and tools used, ma-/maka- for ability and the involuntary, the fixed order of the enclitic particles, ay inversion, comparison, the pseudo-verbs, may and mayroon, both number systems, and the three-way deictics.

lists.title: Tagalog B2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Causatives with magpa- and pa-...-in, the recent perfective that says 'just now', nominalisation with pag- and ka-...-an, relative clauses locked to focus, conditionals, reciprocal and social affixes, and pang- instruments.

lists.title: Tagalog C1 Grammar Path
lists.description: Register across formal Filipino, deep Tagalog and Taglish; focus choice as information structure; and the aspect particles na and pa that the verb form alone cannot carry.

lists.title: Tagalog C2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Literary Filipino and its older particles, affixed words that have drifted from their roots, and code-switching as a rule-governed system rather than a lapse.

points.title: The ang phrase marks the sentence's topic
points.function: Identify what the sentence is 'about'
points.explanation: Tagalog doesn't have a fixed "subject" the way English does. Instead, one noun phrase — marked by ang — is the TOPIC: the participant the sentence is "about," chosen by which role the verb's affix highlights. Kumain ang bata ("The child ate") marks the eater (bata) as topic because kumain is an actor-focus verb.

drills.hint: ang — marks the actor as the topic, since kumain is actor-focus
ang — the drinker is the topic here
ang — marks the topic noun phrase

points.title: ng marks a non-topic actor, object, or possessor
points.function: Mark a noun that isn't the topic
points.explanation: ng (pronounced "nang") marks a noun phrase that ISN'T the topic — often the object when the actor is topic, or a possessor: Kumain ang bata ng pagkain ("The child ate [some] food") marks pagkain with ng because it's the object, not the topic. The same ng also shows possession: bahay ng kaibigan ("friend's house").

drills.hint: ng — marks the object, since it isn't the topic here
ng — also marks a possessor: "house OF friend"

points.title: sa marks location, direction, or a specific place
points.function: Say where something happens
points.explanation: sa introduces location or direction — "in," "at," "to": Pumunta ang bata sa bahay ("The child went to the house"). It's also used for definite/specific places and times.

drills.translation: The child went to the house.
The man drank at the house.

points.title: Actor-focus verbs with the -um- infix
points.function: Build actor-focus verbs from a root
points.explanation: Many Tagalog action verbs form their actor-focus version by inserting -um- right after the root's first consonant: kain ("eat") → kumain; bili ("buy") → bumili. If the root starts with a vowel, -um- simply attaches to the front instead: inom ("drink") → uminom.

drills.hint: ate — kain + -um- infix after the first consonant
drank — inom + -um-, attaches to the front since the root starts with a vowel

points.title: The linker na
points.function: Connect a describing word to what it describes
points.explanation: na links a describing word to what it describes, in either order — noun + na + adjective: bata na mabuti ("a good child"). In fast speech na often shortens to -ng and attaches to the previous word if it ends in a vowel (batang mabuti), but na is the safe default to write.

drills.hint: na — links the noun to the adjective that follows
na — the linker between noun and adjective

points.title: mga marks the plural
points.function: Make a noun plural
points.explanation: Tagalog nouns don't change form for plural — instead, the particle mga (pronounced "mah-NGA") goes right before the noun: bata ("child") → mga bata ("children"); bahay ("house") → mga bahay ("houses").

drills.hint: mga — plural marker, placed before the noun
mga — same marker makes any noun plural

points.title: Existence and possession: may and wala
points.function: Say that something exists, or that you have it
points.explanation: may states that something exists or that someone has something: May pagkain ako, literally "there-is food I," means "I have food." Its negative wala works a little differently — it needs the linker -ng on the pronoun: Wala akong pagkain ("I have no food"), not "wala pagkain ako."

drills.hint: may — states existence/possession; "ako" (I) follows the noun
wala — the negative of may; note the pronoun takes the -ng linker (akong)

points.title: hindi negates verbs and adjectives
points.function: Say what isn't true or didn't happen
points.explanation: hindi is the general negator for verbs and adjectives — placed right before what it negates: Hindi kumain ang bata ("The child didn't eat"), Hindi malaki ang bahay ("The house isn't big").

drills.hint: hindi — negates the verb, placed right before it

points.title: mag- actor-focus verbs, beside -um-
points.function: Use the other actor-focus prefix, and hear the difference
points.explanation: mag- is the second big actor-focus affix: magluto 'cook', magbasa 'read', maglinis 'clean'. Many roots take both -um- and mag- with a real difference: bumili 'buy (for oneself)' vs magbili 'sell'; umalis 'leave' vs mag-alis 'remove something'. Broadly -um- leans toward the actor experiencing the action and mag- toward the actor doing something deliberate or repeated — but the pairs are learned word by word.

drills.translation: I clean the house every Saturday.
The child played at the park.

points.title: Aspect: completed, incompleted, contemplated
points.function: Mark when the action stands, not when it happened
points.explanation: Tagalog verbs mark ASPECT, not tense. Three forms: completed (begun and finished — kumain, nagluto), incompleted (begun, still going — kumakain, nagluluto), contemplated (not yet begun — kakain, magluluto). For -um- verbs the incompleted and contemplated reduplicate the first syllable of the root; for mag- verbs the prefix becomes nag-/nagCV-/magCV-. The same form covers English past and present perfect.

points.title: Object focus with -in
points.function: Make the thing acted on the topic
points.explanation: When the OBJECT is the topic, the verb takes -in and the object gets ang: Kinain ko ang mansanas 'I ate the apple' — literally 'the apple was eaten by me'. The actor moves to a ng pronoun (ko, mo, niya). Object focus is the normal choice when the object is definite, which is far more often than English passive would be used.

points.title: Locative focus with -an
points.function: Make the place or recipient the topic
points.explanation: -an puts the LOCATION, direction, or recipient in topic position: Binilhan ko ang tindahan 'I bought from the store'; Pinuntahan namin ang museo 'We went to the museum'. Compare with -in, which makes the thing itself the topic. Choosing the focus is choosing what the sentence is about.

drills.hint: bili + -an — the store is the topic

drills.translation: She gave the child a gift.

points.title: ang pronouns
points.function: Use the pronouns that take the topic slot
points.explanation: The ang set replaces an ang phrase: ako 'I', ka/ikaw 'you', siya 'he/she', kami 'we (not you)', tayo 'we (including you)', kayo 'you (pl/polite)', sila 'they'. ka goes after the verb, ikaw goes first. Tagalog splits 'we' the way Indonesian does — kami excludes the listener, tayo includes them.

drills.translation: We (you and I) will go to Baguio tomorrow.

points.title: ng pronouns
points.function: Say who did it when the object is the topic
points.explanation: The ng set marks a non-topic actor or a possessor: ko 'I/my', mo 'you/your', niya 'he/his, she/her', namin 'our (excl)', natin 'our (incl)', ninyo 'your (pl)', nila 'their'. In object-focus sentences the actor is always a ng pronoun: Kinain KO ang mansanas. As possessors they follow the noun: bahay ko 'my house'.

points.title: sa pronouns and possession
points.function: Say to me, for you, and mine
points.explanation: The sa set marks a location, recipient, or emphatic possessor: akin 'me/mine', iyo 'you/yours', kaniya 'him/her/theirs', amin, atin, inyo, kanila. With sa they give direction (sa akin 'to me'); alone and fronted they possess emphatically (Akin ang bahay 'The house is MINE'). Everyday possession still uses the ng set after the noun.

points.title: si and sina: names take their own marker
points.function: Mark people's names correctly
points.explanation: Personal names never take ang. They take si (singular) and sina (plural) in the topic slot, ni/nina as non-topic actor or possessor, and kay/kina after sa. Using ang with a name is one of the most audible learner errors: *ang Maria is simply wrong; si Maria is right.

drills.hint: si — topic marker for a name
kay — sa form for a name

points.title: Questions: ba and the question words
points.function: Ask yes/no and wh- questions
points.explanation: ba turns any statement into a yes/no question and sits after the first word or phrase: Kumain ka ba? Question words come first and are usually followed by ang or a linker: ano 'what', sino 'who', saan 'where', kailan 'when', bakit 'why', paano 'how', magkano 'how much', ilan 'how many'.

points.title: ma- adjectives and the linker
points.function: Describe things and attach the description
points.explanation: Most descriptive words take ma-: maganda 'beautiful', mabait 'kind', malaki 'big', mabilis 'fast'. To attach one to a noun you need the linker: -ng after a vowel (magandang bahay), na after a consonant (bahay na maganda). Either order works — what is not optional is the linker.

drills.translation: They live in a beautiful house.

drills.hint: malaki as predicate — no linker needed

points.title: i- focus: benefactive and instrument
points.function: Make the thing given, or the tool, the topic
points.explanation: i- puts the thing transferred, the beneficiary's object, or the instrument in the topic slot: Ibinigay ko ang libro 'I gave the book'; Ipinambili ko ang pera 'I used the money to buy'. Compare the three: Binigyan ko ang bata (the CHILD is topic, -an) vs Ibinigay ko ang libro (the BOOK is topic, i-).

drills.hint: i- + bigay — the book is the topic

drills.translation: He used the new knife to cut.
I threw out the rubbish earlier.

points.title: ma- and maka-: ability and the involuntary
points.function: Say could, managed to, and happened to
points.explanation: ma- and maka- mark ability or an unintended action: nakita ko 'I saw / happened to see' (versus tiningnan ko 'I looked at'); narinig 'heard' vs pinakinggan 'listened to'; nakapunta 'managed to go'. Perception verbs live almost entirely in this set — you rarely 'deliberately see'.

drills.translation: I didn't hear what you said.

drills.sentence: {{answer}} ako sa Maynila noong isang taon.
drills.translation: I managed to go to Manila last year.

points.title: Enclitic particles and their order
points.function: Place na, pa, ba, po and daw correctly
points.explanation: Tagalog has a set of little words that cling after the first stressed word, in a fixed order: na 'already/now', pa 'still/yet', ba (question), po/ho (respect), daw/raw 'reportedly', naman (contrast/softener), kasi 'because', nga 'indeed'. Kumain na ba kayo? Getting the ORDER wrong is what marks a learner more than any single word choice.

drills.translation: The weather is nice, they say.

points.title: ay inversion
points.function: Write the formal, subject-first order
points.explanation: Default Tagalog is predicate-first: Maganda ang bahay. Fronting the topic requires the marker ay: Ang bahay ay maganda. This is the register of writing, speeches and formal instruction — everyday speech uses it sparingly. In writing ay is often contracted to 'y after a vowel: Ako'y masaya.

points.title: Comparison: mas, kaysa, pinaka-
points.function: Say more, than, and most
points.explanation: mas X (kaysa sa Y) is 'more X than Y': Mas mataas siya kaysa sa akin. The superlative is pinaka-: pinakamaganda 'most beautiful', pinakamalaki 'biggest'. Equality uses kasing-/sing-: kasingtaas 'as tall as'. mas is a Spanish loan and is now completely standard.

drills.translation: She is the smartest in the class.
He is as tall as me.
This is the biggest house on the street.

points.title: Pseudo-verbs: gusto, ayaw, dapat, puwede
points.function: Say want, don't want, should, may
points.explanation: These take no aspect of their own and are followed by a ng pronoun plus a verb: Gusto kong kumain 'I want to eat' (note the linker -ng on gusto). ayaw 'not want', kailangan 'need', dapat 'should', puwede/maaari 'may, can', kaya 'be able'. With a noun they take the ng set directly: Gusto ko ng kape.

points.title: may and mayroon
points.function: Say there is, and have
points.explanation: may goes straight before the thing (May aso ako 'I have a dog'); mayroon/meron is used when a pronoun or particle comes between (Mayroon akong aso), and stands alone as an answer (Mayroon! 'There is!'). The negative for both is wala.

points.title: Counting: native and Spanish numbers
points.function: Use the right number system for the job
points.explanation: Tagalog keeps two sets. Native (isa, dalawa, tatlo…) is used for counting things, ages and general quantity. Spanish-derived (uno, dos, tres…, and singko, diyes, bente) dominates time, money and prices — alas-dos 'two o'clock', bente pesos. Using native numbers for money sounds odd; using Spanish ones for 'three children' sounds odd too.

points.title: Deictics: ito, iyan, iyon
points.function: Point at things by distance from the speaker
points.explanation: Three degrees, not two: ito 'this (near me)', iyan 'that (near you)', iyon 'that (far from both)'. They inflect like ang-phrases — nito/niyan/niyon for the ng set, dito/diyan/doon for place. The three-way split maps onto the speaker/listener/elsewhere distinction, not simple distance.

drills.translation: The price of this is high.

points.title: Causatives: magpa- and pa-...-in
points.function: Say you had someone do something
points.explanation: magpa- makes the causer the topic (Nagpaluto ako ng pagkain 'I had food cooked'); pa-...-in makes the person made to act the topic (Pinaluto ko siya 'I made him cook'); ipa- makes the thing the topic (Ipinaluto ko ang isda). Filipino uses causatives where English says 'have someone do' or 'get something done', and it is far more frequent than the English equivalent.

drills.hint: magpa- + gawa — the causer is topic

drills.translation: I had the clothes washed by the laundrywoman.
He had himself examined by a doctor.

points.title: Recent perfective: ka- + reduplication
points.function: Say something has only just happened
points.explanation: A distinct aspect English has no single form for: ka- plus reduplication of the first syllable means the action finished a moment ago. Kakakain ko lang 'I just ate'; Kararating lang niya 'He's only just arrived'. It is almost always accompanied by lang. Learners tend to reach for the completed aspect and lose the 'just now' that Tagalog states outright.

points.title: Nominalisation: pag-, pagka-, ka-...-an
points.function: Turn actions and qualities into nouns
points.explanation: pag- + root names the act (pagkain 'eating, food', pag-aaral 'studying'); pagka- names the manner or the state of having done it (pagkakain 'the way of eating', pagkatapos 'after'); ka-...-an names abstractions (kaganda-han 'beauty', kalayaan 'freedom', kabaitan 'kindness'). Formal Filipino writing is built from these.

drills.translation: She is known for her kindness.

points.title: Relative clauses with na and -ng
points.function: Attach a whole clause to a noun
points.explanation: The same linker that joins an adjective joins a clause: ang taong kumain 'the person who ate', ang librong binasa ko 'the book that I read'. The verb inside the clause must be in the focus that makes the head noun its topic — you cannot say *ang librong bumasa ako, because bumasa makes the READER the topic. Focus and relativisation are locked together.

drills.sentence: Ang libro{{answer}} binasa ko ay maganda.
drills.translation: The book I read is good.

drills.sentence: Ang bahay {{answer}} tinitirhan nila ay malaki.
drills.translation: The house they live in is big.

drills.sentence: Ang babae{{answer}} nagluto ay nanay ko.
drills.translation: The woman who cooked is my mother.
drills.hint: actor focus — she is the topic

points.title: Conditionals: kung, kapag, sana
points.function: Say if, when, and if only
points.explanation: kung is 'if' for uncertain conditions and also 'whether'; kapag/pag is 'when(ever)' for things expected to happen. sana carries the wish or counterfactual: Sana umulan 'I hope it rains'; Kung mayaman ako, sana… 'If I were rich…'. Tagalog puts the unreality in sana, not in the verb.

drills.translation: If it rains, I won't go.
Whenever I go home, I call.
I don't know whether he'll come.

points.title: Reciprocal and social affixes
points.function: Say to each other, and to go along with
points.explanation: mag-...-an makes an action mutual: magkita 'meet each other', magtulungan 'help one another', mag-usap 'talk to each other'. makipag- means joining in with someone: makipag-usap 'converse with', makipaglaro 'play with'. These carry the social texture of Filipino, where doing things together is grammatically marked rather than just implied.

drills.translation: They helped one another during the storm.
I want to talk with him.
The children are playing with each other.

points.title: pang- instruments and other noun prefixes
points.function: Name the tool and the season
points.explanation: pang- (pam-/pan- by the same nasal rule as Indonesian's meN-) names an instrument: panulat 'writing tool', pambura 'eraser', panghiwa 'cutter'. tag- names a season or period: tag-ulan 'rainy season', tag-init 'hot season', taglamig 'cold season'. ka- names a partner or counterpart: kaibigan 'friend', kapatid 'sibling', katrabaho 'workmate'.

drills.translation: The pen is on the table.
The rain is heavy during the rainy season.
He is my workmate at the office.

points.title: Register: Filipino, deep Tagalog, and Taglish
points.function: Move between the three registers educated speakers use
points.explanation: Three registers coexist. Formal Filipino (news, school) prefers ay-inversion and native coinages. Deep or 'malalim' Tagalog uses words most urban speakers now find literary — salumpuwit for upuan, and the older particles. Taglish mixes English freely (Nag-aral ako ng math kanina) and is the everyday register of Metro Manila, including among the highly educated. Choosing wrongly is what marks a foreigner long after the grammar is right.

drills.translation: The child is diligent in studying.

drills.hint: Taglish — English noun in Tagalog frame
Taglish verbalisation of an English noun

points.title: Focus choice as information structure
points.function: Pick the focus that puts the right thing in view
points.explanation: Focus is not style — it decides what the sentence is ABOUT and which noun is definite. Bumili ako ng libro 'I bought a book' (indefinite book, actor in view); Binili ko ang libro 'I bought the book' (definite book, the book in view). A definite object nearly forces object focus. This is the deepest difference from European languages and the last thing learners get right.

drills.translation: I bought a book at the store.
drills.hint: actor focus — the book is indefinite
object focus — the book is definite

drills.translation: He gave the money to the child.
drills.hint: i- — the money is in view

points.title: Aspect subtleties: na, pa, and the contemplated
points.function: Say already, still, and not-yet precisely
points.explanation: na and pa do work the verb form alone cannot. Kumakain pa siya 'He's still eating' vs Kumain na siya 'He has eaten'. Hindi pa 'not yet' contrasts with hindi 'not at all'. With the contemplated aspect, na means 'now, at last': Aalis na ako 'I'm leaving now'. Aspect plus particle is one system, and translating each half separately produces sentences that are grammatical and wrong.

drills.hint: hindi pa — not yet, still expected

points.title: Literary and formal Filipino
points.function: Read the register of literature and official texts
points.explanation: Literary Filipino keeps forms that everyday speech has shed: ay-inversion throughout, nga and kay as intensifiers (Kay ganda! 'How beautiful!'), ani 'said', the older -in- infix placements, and native coinages minted to replace Spanish and English loans. National literature, the constitution and formal oratory all live here, and none of it sounds like the street.

drills.hint: ay — sustained inversion in formal prose

points.title: Lexicalised affixation
points.function: Recognise affixed words that have left their roots behind
points.explanation: Many affixed Tagalog words no longer mean the sum of their parts. kapatid 'sibling' is not a live ka- + patid; pagkain means 'food', not only 'the act of eating'; magulang 'parent' has drifted from ulang; kasama can be 'companion' or 'included' depending on context. Decomposing these confidently is the reliable way to be wrong.

drills.translation: Tax is included in the price.

drills.hint: magulang — a noun in its own right

points.title: Code-switching as a system
points.function: Switch languages mid-sentence the way bilinguals do
points.explanation: Taglish is rule-governed, not random. English content words slot into Tagalog frames with Tagalog affixes (nag-drive, i-check, na-stress), while the grammatical skeleton — markers, pronouns, aspect, particles — stays Tagalog. The switch tracks topic and formality: technical and professional material tilts English, feeling and family tilt Tagalog, often inside one sentence. Producing this naturally is the final register skill.

drills.hint: i- focus prefix on an English root
i- + English root after a pseudo-verb
